summary: Enumerates the types of events that could be reported by a message store and defines how to report them as notifications, supporting server-to-server and server-to-client notification of things like new mail. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of repeatedly checking your mailbox, the mailbox could ring a bell when something happens. This memo lists the kinds of bells and what they mean.

questions: how do mail servers notify about new messages
what is a message store event
what events does an imap server report
subtitle: A common list of the things a mail store can report, such as new mail, deleted messages and quota changes.

tldr.problem: Internet mail standards had no way for a message store to tell other servers or clients about events such as new messages, and growing demand from mobile devices, voice mail and auditing systems called for an interoperable one.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC enumerates event types in four groups (message addition and deletion, message flags, access accounting, mailbox management) and the parameters each can carry, and sets up an IANA registry so both can be extended.
tldr.outcome: It defines what events mean, not how they travel. A transport or message format has to be specified elsewhere, and it is not a replacement for IMAP.

today: RFC 5423 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the events and parameters; the RFC leaves message formats and transport bindings to other documents.

sections.title: Why Message Stores Need Events
sections.content:
A message store organizes Internet messages into mailboxes and gives access to them. Remote access came through POP, IMAP and web mail built on HTTP. Simple notification tricks existed, such as the IMAP IDLE command (RFC 2177) and Simple New Mail Notification (RFC 4146), but the RFC says demand was growing for something more complete.

It lists the drivers: mobile devices with intermittent connectivity and new-mail indicators, unified messaging with phone message-waiting lights, event-based billing, passing events to non-Internet notification systems, calendar systems subscribing to MessageNew, and legal auditing requirements in some jurisdictions.

This is a first step: it lists the core events that real-world customers demand, including those that IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501) and some extensions can generate. It is not intended as a replacement for a message access facility such as IMAP.
sections.plainLanguage: People want their phone to buzz when new mail arrives, without it asking over and over. To do that, everyone first needs to agree on what the buzzes mean.

sections.title: The Event Model
sections.content:
The model of a message store is the one implicit in IMAP4rev1 and its extensions. An event typically has a mailbox name and usually a user name (an authorization identity in SASL terms). An event about one message can use an IMAP URL, and an event about a set of messages can use an IMAP URL to the mailbox plus a set of IMAP UIDs.

Every notification has a type and parameters. Types and parameter names are limited to US-ASCII printable characters so they map easily onto any notification system. The RFC does not say which parameters are mandatory or optional; that is left to documents that define concrete message formats or bindings.

UIDVALIDITY matters here: when it changes, a caching client MUST flush its cache, so it must be included with events about message addition or removal.

For scalability, some filtering at event generation is needed, at least switching groups of related events on and off and suppressing large parameters such as messageContent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bell has a name, like "new letter", plus a note saying which mailbox, whose, and what changed.

sections.title: Message Addition, Deletion and Quota Events
sections.content:
Several events cover messages arriving and leaving:

  • MessageNew: a message was received via a message delivery agent. Parameters MUST include UIDVALIDITY and a UID for IMAP-accessible stores, and may include the SMTP envelope, metadata or even the whole message. One suggested policy is to include messages up to 2K in size and use a URLAUTH reference for larger ones.
  • MessageAppend: a client appended a message; like MessageNew but without the SMTP envelope.
  • MessageExpire: messages were removed by server expiration policy.
  • MessageExpunge: messages were expunged by an action such as IMAP CLOSE/EXPUNGE or POP3 DELE+QUIT.

Three quota events follow. QuotaExceed means an operation, typically MessageNew, failed because a quota was exceeded. QuotaWithin means an operation such as an expunge brought usage back under the limit. QuotaChange means the quota itself was changed.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a bell for a new letter, one for a letter thrown away, and one for "your mailbox is full" or "you have room again".

sections.title: Flag, Access and Mailbox Events
sections.content:
Flag events: MessageRead and MessageTrash report messages marked as read or marked for future deletion. POP has no read concept, so MessageRead comes only from IMAP, HTTP or equivalent clients. FlagsSet and FlagsClear report IMAP flags or keywords changing; the flag names MUST NOT include \Recent. By default the simpler MessageRead and MessageTrash forms SHOULD be used for the \Seen and \Deleted flags, and this SHOULD be configurable.

Access accounting: Login and Logout report users connecting and disconnecting via IMAP, HTTP, POP or another mechanism. Logout may carry a disconnect type, with suggested values graceful, abort, timeout and security layer error.

Mailbox management: MailboxCreate, MailboxDelete, MailboxRename, MailboxSubscribe and MailboxUnSubscribe. Implied changes are not reported separately: creating or renaming a mailbox with parents or children does not generate extra events for them.
sections.plainLanguage: More bells tell you a letter was read, someone came in or left, or a folder was made, renamed or removed.

sections.title: Event Parameters
sections.content:
Parameters carry the details. Some are attached to nearly everything: uri (a reference to the IMAP server, mailbox or message) is included with all notifications, and user (the authorization identifier) is included with all events generated by message access protocols, along with clientIP and clientPort.

Others fit particular events. diskQuota and diskUsed are in kilobytes (1024 octets). uidset lists affected UIDs, flagNames lists flags, mailboxID and oldMailboxID are URIs, and messageSize gives the RFC 5322 message size in octets. modseq is the 64-bit MODSEQ from RFC 4551. timestamp uses local time with a UTC offset, normally in RFC 3339 format.

Many may be included with any notification, such as pid, process, serverFQDN, service (suggested values imap, pop, http, admincli) and tags.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bell can come with a little note: who, which mailbox, how big, and when it happened.

sections.title: The IANA Registry and Future Extensions
sections.content:
IANA created a registry called Internet Message Store Events with two sub-registries, for event names and for event parameters. Entries not starting with vnd. are for interoperable use and are allocated by IETF Consensus. Entries starting with vnd. are for private use and allocated First Come First Served.

Appendix A says the core events were chosen because they are well understood, have known use cases and are implemented by at least one deployed message store. The exceptions are FlagsSet, FlagsClear and the mailbox management events. Postponed ideas include moves to archive storage, quota by message context, authentication failure, disabled accounts, annotations and mailbox ACL or metadata changes.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of bell names. Anyone can add their own private ones if they start the name with "vnd.".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Notifications can produce a lot of traffic and expose sensitive information. If notifications keep different systems in step, an attacker who can corrupt them could manipulate those systems. The RFC's example: altering the user and messageContent parameters of MessageNew notifications sent to an auditing server would create false audit log entries.

A transport for notifications must consider authentication, authorization, privacy, message integrity and denial of service. Publish/subscribe systems more complex than a single end-to-end TCP connection need extra care.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone could fake the bells, they could trick the people listening. So the way bells are delivered has to be protected.
